title: Wood and Its Impact on Humans and Environment Quality in Health Care Facilities
research_question: To investigate the impact of natural materials, particularly wood, on human well-being and environmental quality in health care facilities, specifically focusing on physiological responses, emotional states, and indoor environmental quality.

participants.description: 50 volunteers (40 for ECG: 24 men, 16 women, mean age 27.6 ± 9.5 years, 38 right-handed; 4 for EEG: 3 men, 1 woman, mean age 26.3 ± 4.8 years, all right-handed; all 50 for face emotions). Participants were moving in the waiting room for 20 min.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies volunteers for an experiment.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A renovated wooden waiting room at the National Oncology Institute in Bratislava. It featured wall paneling and ceiling cladding made of solid pine wood, seating area of larch timber, secondary veneering with pinewood veneer, and new warm white lighting. Compared to the same room prior to reconstruction (old waiting room).

measures.instrument: Salivary ELISA cortisol kit (DRG instruments GmbH)
4 IP cameras, FaceMedia ACSS technology (based on FACS)

mechanisms: Antimicrobial properties of wood due to tannins and terpenoids.
Wood's anatomical structure not supporting microorganism reproduction.
Wood's 'sink effect' (adsorption and delayed re-emission of VOCs).
Wood as a natural and familiar material reduces stress and calms the brain.
Wood's visual stimuli (patterns) and olfactory properties (smell) engage human perception positively.
Wood influences the sensomotoric cortex, particularly the left hemisphere (analytic thinking/logic).
The 'wow effect' of initial contact with wood leading to mild physiological arousal.
Parasympathetic nervous activity enhancement and sympathetic activity decrease in wooden environments.
implementation_implications: Zone inner spaces of health care facilities to use wood and other naturally porous materials only in less exposed areas.
Use oils, waxes, and lacquers on intensively used surfaces, while leaving other surfaces without finishing.
Educate architects and interior designers about the benefits of using wood in hospital spaces, education, and working facilities.
Develop standardized wooden products and interiors to make tailored design less expensive.
Regular cleaning with ethanol is more efficient for maintaining hygiene and antimicrobial properties of wood.

Overall number of colony-forming units (CFU) of microorganisms on the surfaces (determined by the swabbing method).
Overall number of colony-forming units (CFU) of microorganisms on surfaces (determined by contact plates method).
Testing of the surface by the swabbing method in relation to the possibilities of cleaning and maintenance 4 months after installation of wooden elements.
VOC (volatile organic compound) emissions evaluated in the waiting area.

limitations: The study notes a general lack of articles on methods for measuring environmental effects on humans, suggesting a need for more relevant tools.
Different exposure times might be needed for synchronization to reach a critical point for physiological responses, suggesting a methodological refinement for future studies.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The paper presents the application of natural materials, especially wood, which are relevant for human well-being in built environments of health, social, and day care facilities. These properties were tested by a complex methodology in a case study in the wooden waiting room at National Oncology Institute in Bratislava. In this space, experimental tests of physiological responses were further executed on 50 volunteers moving in the waiting room for 20 min. In this article, the EEG (electroencephalograph) (four persons) and emotions from the faces of all our volunteers before entering and after a stay in a wooden waiting room were recorded. Specifically, the ECG (electrocardiograph), heart rate (HR), and respiration activity were measured by using our own designed ECG holter (40 persons), and also blood pressure and cortisol levels were observed. The usage of wooden materials verifies their regenerative and positive impact on the human nervous system, through the appealing aesthetics (color, texture, and structures), high contact comfort, pleasant smell, possibility to regulate air humidity, volatile organic compound emissions (VOC-emissions), and acoustic well-being in the space.
